title: What is known about 1RB1RA_0LC0RE_1LF1LD_1LA0LA_1LC1RB_---1LC
description: Proof status of the six-state BB(6) holdout 1RB1RA_0LC0RE_1LF1LD_1LA0LA_1LC1RB_---1LC.
intro: Nobody knows whether this six-state, two-symbol Turing machine halts when started on a blank tape. Its run is an odometer with three wheels; it can only halt at the moment the slowest wheel turns over, and only if the fastest one is at one exact position then.
verdict: The question is open. Every time the head reaches a new cell on the right in state B the tape is S(c, a, b) = (10)^c 1^a 0 (10)^b 1 B>0, and a three-line rule (checked against direct simulation) gives the next one: the right block doubles while the pool can pay, a carry turns a pair of the left block into pool, and when the left block is empty the pool becomes the new left block (a reset). With u = b + 1 and v = a/2 + b + 2 this is exactly a doubling map, u ↦ 2u modulo v, whose modulus grows by one at every operation; c counts the wrap-arounds left before the next reset. The machine halts iff a reset happens with 2u = v exactly, and this equivalence is now a theorem checked by Lean's kernel, for the exact map and from blank tape, with nothing about the run assumed.

Why a halt is unlikely. The exact map run for 1011 operations (5·1010 visits, far beyond 1030 machine steps) makes 54 resets, none halting; the left block now has tens of billions of pairs. At a reset 2u − v is spread over about v/2 values and one of them halts; the moduli grow geometrically from reset to reset, so the chance of any later halt is about 10−10. That same growth makes resets logarithmically rare (reset k needs about 1.47k operations), and the doubling map has no known shortcut or invariant, so neither a much longer run nor a proof is in sight.

claims.title: The halting configurations
claims.text: The machine stops exactly when it reads the symbol of a halting transition (F0); the generated statement covers every configuration.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10,000 steps
claims.text: The list simulator of the shared library, proved to agree with the machine's semantics, runs 10,000 steps from blank tape without a halt, evaluated by Lean's kernel.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps
claims.text: The same run, evaluated by compiled code.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>9</sup> steps
claims.text: The C simulator tools/c/triage.c runs 109 steps without a halt; at the end 4,166 cells have been visited and 3,725 of them hold a 1.

claims.title: The odometer rule
claims.text: For S(c, a, b) = 0^∞ (10)^c 1^a 0 (10)^b 1 B>0 0^∞ with a even and a ≥ 2, the next right-end visit in state B is: if 2b < a, S(c, a − 2b, 2b + 1) (the right block doubles, eating 1s); if 2b ≥ a and c ≥ 1, apply the rule to (c − 1, 2a + 4, max(b − a/2 − 1, 0)) (a carry: one 10 of the left block becomes 1s); if 2b ≥ a and c = 0, halt when b = a/2 and otherwise apply the rule to (a, 4, b − a/2 − 1) (a reset: the 1s become the new left block). Checked against direct simulation for all c < 6, even 2 ≤ a < 30, b < 34 (2,856 configurations), and on every such visit in the first 3·10<sup>6</sup> steps of the run, which first reaches S(0, 4, 1) at step 43.

claims.title: It halts iff the doubling map halts
claims.text: HaltsFromBlank ↔ ∃ n, opIter n (0, 2, 5) = none, where op is the doubling map on (c, u, v) below. Two layers: the machine halts iff the orbit of the visit S(0, 4, 1) (step 43) under the visit map F reaches none (every value of F proved on the tape, for every visit, from the rules of Rules.lean); and, by arithmetic, one step of F is one or more operations of op, with a halt exactly when op halts.

claims.title: The building blocks of the odometer, for all parameters
claims.text: Each move between two visits is a Lean theorem about every value of its counts and every tape in its context: the start of a sweep, a round (two 1s of the pool and one pair of the right block become four 1s of the middle block), the end of a sweep (the doubled block), the carry (a pair of the left block and the middle block become the new pool), the reset (the middle block becomes the new left block), and the boundary cases: a pool of two, a carry with two, one or no pairs of the right block left (the last is the emptying carry), a reset with one pair left.

claims.title: The exact-hit reset halts
claims.text: With pool, left block and right block all empty (0^∞ A> 1 0 1^(4n+1) 0 1^4 0^∞) the machine fills the tape with 1s and stops on the undefined transition (F reading 0), for every n.

claims.title: The odometer is a doubling map
claims.text: With u = b + 1 and v = a/2 + b + 2: 2u < v is a visit with (2u, v + 1); 2u > v is a carry to (2u − v, v + 1) that uses one unit of c, or with c = 0 a reset to c = 2(v − u − 1), u = 2u − v, v = u + 3; 2u = v is a carry to (1, v + 2), or with c = 0 the halt. Proved for every visit (F_op), and evaluated: no halt in the first 104 operations (kernel) and 107 (native_decide). v + c = 5 + visits + resets + emptying carries.

claims.title: 54 resets, no halt
claims.text: The doubling map in C (the same first 50,000 visits and the same resets as the Python model) runs 10<sup>11</sup> operations, 50,000,165,924 visits, 54 resets, without a halt. Reset 54 happens at v = 35,143,437,691 with 2u − v = 1,095,845,857 and makes a left block of 34,047,591,832. The smallest (2u − v)/v at a reset is 0.028 (reset 11).

claims.title: A later halt has probability about 10<sup>−10</sup>
claims.text: At a reset 2u − v is one of about v/2 values, one of which halts. The moduli at resets grow by a factor between 1 and 2 (about 1.47 on average), so the chances form a geometric series: about 6/v after a reset at v, 10<sup>−10</sup> after reset 54. The same growth is why resets are logarithmically rare: reset k needs about 1.47<sup>k</sup> operations.

claims.title: Why no invariant is in sight
claims.text: Every lap starts at u = v − 3, so a lap is a function of its modulus; its pattern of wrap-arounds is the binary expansion of a real number within 1/v of u/v, and an exact hit is a long run of zeros in that expansion, to the exact integer. Backwards, a state has exactly one predecessor when v is even, and two or none (u even or odd) when v is odd: the backward tree of the halting states is a critical branching process, which is where the 1/v density comes from. Every class of (u, v, c) modulo 8 contains states that halt, so no invariant modulo a power of 2 can rule the halt out.

claims.title: Does a reset ever land on 2u = v (b = a/2)?
claims.text: No congruence excludes it: the halting state has predecessors under the map for every even v. Deciding the machine means deciding a chaotic doubling map with a moving modulus.

explainer.lede: Nobody knows whether it halts. The tape is an odometer with three wheels: a fast one that doubles, a middle one that ticks down, and a slow one that resets. In numbers it doubles a counter u modulo a modulus v that grows by one each time. The machine can only halt at a reset, and only if the doubling lands exactly on v at that moment. In 54 resets that has never happened, and the target keeps getting smaller. Below, each level of that description has its own interactive picture, and at the end the whole question is one five-line definition.

facts.text: The odometer as a doubling map; v grows by one each operation.
No halt in 10<sup>11</sup> operations of the exact map.

sections.heading: The tape at its visits
html: Every time the head steps onto a cell no earlier step has reached, on the right and in state B, the tape is
a left block of c pairs 10, a pool of a ones, a single 0, a right block of b
pairs, and a final 1 with the head just after it. Between two visits the head sweeps back to the left end of the
right block and works its way out again. Inside a sweep the tape is
with a middle block of 4k + 1 ones growing between the pool and what is left of the right block. Every
move of the sweep is a Lean theorem for all values of its counts (lean/Rules.lean):
• A round (round): two 1s of the pool and one pair of the right block become four 1s of the
middle block. It costs 8k + 8 steps, because the head crosses the middle block, so a whole sweep costs of the order
• The end of the sweep (final_g): when the right block is used up, the middle block is
rewritten as a right block twice as long, and the head reaches new ground: the next visit is
two, one or no pairs of the right block are left): when the pool runs out first, one pair of the left block is
used up and the middle block becomes the new pool, which is why the pool jumps from a to 2a + 4.
• A reset (reset, reset_z1): when the pool runs out and the left block is
already empty, the middle block is rewritten as a new left block and a fresh pool of four 1s starts.
• The halt (halt_R): if pool, left block and right block all run out in the same round, the
head walks into the blank left part in state F and finds the undefined transition.

one moment, time running downwards; the coloured bands at the top and bottom are the blocks of the two visits.
The zigzags are the rounds: the head runs back and forth across the middle block, which grows by four cells each

sections.heading: Exact tapes, exact step counts
html:
The same machine written the way the bbchallenge wiki writes Antihydra's: name the tapes exactly, then list the rules, each with the exact number of machine steps it takes. The Lean proof works one level below the doubling map, on the sweep of lean/Map.lean, so the table follows it. Two families of tapes, the visit and a configuration inside a sweep (Lean: S c p b with a = 2p + 2, and Rc c p k z):

The last column names the Lean theorem with that step count: blank_to_S in lean/Map.lean, all others in lean/Rules.lean, each for every value of its counts. The halting row counts the steps up to and including the halting transition: halt_run proves 16k + 30 steps to a tape where F reads 0, which is undefined. lean/Map.lean rewrites these moves onto the tapes S and R (r_start, r_round, …, r_halt) and assembles them into the visit map F; that file keeps the tapes but not the step counts, and halts_iff proves the machine halts iff these rules, started at S(0, 4, 1), reach the halt row. lean/Doubling.lean (halts_iff_op) turns the same rules into the doubling map on (c, u, v) = (c, b + 1, a/2 + b + 2). Every row has also been checked against direct simulation (py/model.py rules): each rule on 3,740 tapes, the chain of rules from 2,856 visits to the next visit or the halt (28 of them halt), and every one of the 377 visits of the first 107 steps of the run, each at the predicted step.

A doubling (2b < a) is one start, b rounds and the end of the sweep: S(c, a, b) → S(c, a − 2b, 2b + 1) in 4b2 + 12b + 24 steps, that is 4u2 + 4u + 16 in the variables of the doubling map. For example S(1, 2, 6), a visit whose next reset halts: the sweep starts (42 steps) at R(1, 0, 0, 5), the pool is already empty so a carry (22) gives R(0, 2, 1, 2), two rounds (16 and 24) give R(0, 0, 3, 0), and with pool, left block and right block all empty the machine halts after 79 more: 183 steps in all, which is what direct simulation gives.

sections.heading: Three wheels
html: Forget the steps and keep only the three numbers c, a, b of each visit. The sweep moves of the previous section
add up to one rule for the next visit (F in lean/Map.lean, proved for every visit):
2b ≥ a, c ≥ 1   carry: go on with (c − 1, 2a + 4, max(b − a/2 − 1, 0))
2b ≥ a, c = 0   halt if b = a/2,
else reset: go on with (a, 4, b − a/2 − 1)
• Fast wheel. If the pool is big enough (2b < a), one sweep doubles the right block, b ↦ 2b + 1,
• Middle wheel. If the pool is too small and c ≥ 1, one pair of the left block is used up: the pool becomes
2a + 4 and b drops by a/2 + 1; then the fast wheel tries again.
• Slow wheel. If the pool is too small and the left block is empty, the whole pool becomes the new left
block (c = a), a new pool of 4 starts, and b drops by a/2 + 1, unless b is exactly a/2: then the machine
So the run is a sequence of resets, each one making a left block as long as the pool was. From blank tape the
first left blocks are 2, 8, 4, 24, 52, 44, 120, …; after 10<sup>11</sup> operations there have been 54 resets and the
latest left block is 34,047,591,832 pairs long.

sections.heading: Doubling modulo a growing number
html: Change variables: put u = b + 1 and v = a/2 + b + 2 (so a = 2(v − u − 1) and b = u − 1). The
odometer's condition 2b < a becomes 2u < v, and its three wheels become one operation on (c, u, v)
<pre>2u < v          u ← 2u,  v ← v + 1                          a visit
2u > v, c ≥ 1   u ← 2u − v,  v ← v + 1,  c ← c − 1          a carry
2u = v, c ≥ 1   u ← 1,  v ← v + 2,  c ← c − 1               an emptying carry
2u > v, c = 0   c ← 2(v − u − 1),  u ← 2u − v,  v ← u + 3   a reset
In words: double u; if that reaches v, subtract v and use up one unit of c; add one to v. So u is doubled
modulo v, and the modulus creeps up by one at every operation. The left block c only counts the wrap-arounds: c of
them are allowed, and the next one is a reset, which refills c with 2(v − u − 1) and drops the modulus to
(2u − v) + 3. The machine halts exactly when a reset finds 2u = v, that is when u sits exactly at the middle
of [0, v] at the moment the left block is empty.
The quantity that matters is the fraction x = u/v. Doubling sends x to about 2x when x < 1/2 and to about
2x − 1 when x > 1/2: the binary shift, the textbook example of chaos. The small corrections from v growing are
what keep it exactly computable and unpredictable at once. One thing is conserved: c + v = 5 + visits + resets +
emptying carries, so the modulus is essentially a clock that counts visits.
The strip shows where u sits in [0, v], with the middle marked; the trail is the last few positions. Step through
operations and watch u jump around, wrap past the middle, and use up the left block.
<svg id="h5d-svg" viewBox="0 0 700 120" style="width:100%;height:auto;display:block;margin-top:12px" role="img" aria-label="u on the interval from 0 to v"></svg>

sections.heading: Laps, and why they get rarer
html: Cut the operations at the resets and call each piece a lap. A reset sets u = 2u − v and then v = u + 3,
so every lap starts at u = v − 3, just below the top of the interval, and its left block c and starting
modulus v satisfy c + v = V + 1, where V is the modulus at the reset that began it. A lap is therefore fixed by two
numbers, its starting modulus and its allowance of wrap-arounds, and it ends at its (c + 1)-th wrap-around, which
is the next reset. The machine halts iff some lap ends with an exact hit, 2u = v at that last
How long a lap lasts depends on how many wrap-arounds it is allowed, and that is set by where the previous reset
landed: a reset that finds 2u − v small makes a long left block and a long next lap. Roughly, a lap starting at
modulus v ends near v(3 − 2x) for a fraction x between 1/2 and 1, so the modulus at a reset grows by a factor
between 1 and 2 from lap to lap: about 1.47 on average in theory, about 1.52 in the 54 laps of the run. This is why
resets are logarithmically rare: reset k comes after about 1.5<sup>k</sup> operations, and 10<sup>11</sup>
The modulus v at each reset
<div style="position:relative"><canvas id="h5l-a" style="display:block;width:100%;height:240px" aria-label="Modulus at each reset, logarithmic scale"></canvas>
Logarithmic scale. The dashed line is the least-squares fit, ×1.52 per reset.
How close each reset came to a halt
<div style="position:relative"><canvas id="h5l-b" style="display:block;width:100%;height:240px" aria-label="Fraction (2u - v)/v at each reset"></canvas>
The fraction (2u − v)/v at the reset; a halt needs exactly 0. The closest call is reset 11, at 0.028.

The wrap-arounds of a lap are binary digits
Write a 1 for each wrap-around of a lap and a 0 for each plain doubling. Doubling modulo a fixed v would give
exactly the binary digits of u/v; because v grows by one at every operation they are instead the digits of a nearby
number x with |v<sub>0</sub>x − u<sub>0</sub>| ≤ 1 (between emptying carries). So the first log<sub>2</sub> v
digits agree with those of u<sub>0</sub>/v<sub>0</sub> and then the two drift apart. The lap ends at its

log<sub>2</sub> v zeros, to the exact integer. Deciding the machine is deciding where an implicitly defined binary
expansion has such a pattern: a question of the same kind as whether a given number is normal, for which there is no

sections.heading: The whole question in one definition
html: Everything above comes down to the following. There is no tape and there are no states left, only three whole
if 2u > v:                      c ← c − 1,  u ← 2u − v,  v ← v + 1
if 2u = v:                      c ← c − 1,  u ← 1,       v ← v + 2
if 2u > v:                      c ← 2(v − u − 1),  u ← 2u − v,  v ← u + 3
Kernel The machine 1RB1RA_0LC0RE_1LF1LD_1LA0LA_1LC1RB_---1LC halts from a
blank tape if and only if this loop stops. (In the reset line the new v uses the new u, so v becomes
2u − v + 3 in terms of the old values.)
The same thing as a recursive definition
Write H(c, u, v) for "the loop stops when started from (c, u, v)". Then H is the predicate defined by
<pre style="font-size:.9rem;margin:0">H(c, u, v) = H(c, 2u, v + 1)                        if 2u < v
H(c, u, v) = H(c − 1, 2u − v, v + 1)                if 2u > v and c ≥ 1
H(c, u, v) = H(c − 1, 1, v + 2)                     if 2u = v and c ≥ 1
H(c, u, v) = H(2(v − u − 1), 2u − v, 2u − v + 3)    if 2u > v and c = 0
H(c, u, v) = true                                   if 2u = v and c = 0
H is defined by unbounded recursion, so "H(0, 2, 5) is false" means "the recursion never terminates". Each case
moves to a state with a larger v except the reset, which can lower it; that is why there is no measure that would
make the recursion obviously finite or obviously infinite.

Since every reset leaves u = v − 3, the loop can also be read as a recursion on laps. Lap(c, v) runs the loop
from (c, v − 3, v) up to its (c + 1)-th wrap-around, the first one with c = 0; say that happens at (0, u, V). If
2u = V the machine halts; otherwise the next lap is Lap(2(V − u − 1), 2u − V + 3). The run from blank tape is lap 1
from (0, 2, 5) followed by Lap(2, 5), Lap(8, 6), Lap(4, 32), Lap(24, 16), …, and its 54th reset is at
This is the definition the theorem is about, copied from lean/Doubling.lean; none is the
<pre>def op : Nat × Nat × Nat → Option (Nat × Nat × Nat)
if 2 * u < v then some (c, 2 * u, v + 1)
| c + 1 => if 2 * u = v then some (c, 1, v + 2) else some (c, 2 * u - v, v + 1)
| 0 => if 2 * u = v then none else some (2 * (v - u - 1), 2 * u - v, 2 * u - v + 3)
def opIter : Nat → Nat × Nat × Nat → Option (Nat × Nat × Nat)
theorem halts_iff_op : HaltsFromBlank ↔ ∃ n, opIter n (0, 2, 5) = none

What is not known is the value of H(0, 2, 5): the loop has been run for 10<sup>11</sup> operations (10<sup>7</sup>
of them inside Lean) without stopping.

explainer.title: An odometer that might stop on one exact number

family: three-wheel odometer = doubling map with a growing modulus
summary: An odometer that is exactly a doubling map: u ↦ 2u modulo v, v growing by one each operation, the left block counting the wrap-arounds allowed before a reset. Proved in Lean (kernel): it halts iff a reset happens with 2u = v. No halt in 10^11 operations (54 resets); heuristically about 10^-10 for a later halt; open.
